subjective: Two male stray kittens of the same age, from the same mother, have received only their first vaccines. Deworming was done for the larger cat but not for the white one. Both cats have skin issues including rashes and itching, with one having round patchy lesions and the other having a cut, red mark, scar, and a lump on the neck. The affected cat is not eating well, showing decreased appetite and some vomiting attempts. The cats are mostly outdoor and difficult to catch. One cat exhibits anxiety and aggression but is calm with the owner. No vomiting or diarrhea reported. No abnormal urination or spraying noted. Owner reports difficulty administering medication and reluctance to visit the vet.
objective: Physical examination revealed rashes and round patchy lesions on the back and legs, with some bleeding noted previously. A lump and scar formation were palpated on the neck of one cat. Temperature recorded at 103.7°F, indicating fever. No respiratory signs observed. No ticks or fleas currently seen, but tick prevention was done a year ago with monthly cotton application. Blood tests and skin samples were taken for fungal and bacterial infection assessment. No other pets in contact. No nasal or ocular discharge noted.
assessment: The cats have dermatological issues likely due to bacterial or fungal infections, possibly complicated by parasitic infestations such as ticks or fleas. The fever suggests systemic involvement or infection. The decreased appetite and lethargy in one cat may be related to the fever or underlying infection. Anxiety and aggression in one cat may be stress-related. Differential diagnoses include bacterial skin infection, fungal infection, parasitic dermatitis, and possible food or environmental allergies. Deworming status is incomplete, which may contribute to skin and systemic issues.
plan: Diagnostic: Perform blood tests to evaluate systemic infection and blood parameters; skin cytology and fungal culture from lesion samples. Therapeutic: Start antibiotic and antifungal topical treatments combining ointment and spray; administer omega-3 and omega-6 fatty acid supplements for skin health; apply monthly spot-on flea and tick treatment for at least three months; recommend deworming syrup administration. Preventive: Maintain yearly vaccination schedule; avoid harsh chemicals in resting areas to protect skin barrier. Monitoring: Keep cats indoors during treatment; separate cats for 30 minutes post-application to prevent licking; monitor temperature and appetite closely. Owner Instructions: Gradually transition food by mixing old and new diets; provide wet food to ensure hydration; complete full antibiotic course if started; attempt to administer medications mixed with food or syrup form; observe for any worsening of symptoms or new signs. Follow-up: Review blood and skin test results in 2-3 hours; plan further diagnostics if no improvement; consider blood tests for hypothyroidism or other systemic causes if skin condition persists.
conclusion: Two male stray kittens presented with dermatological lesions including rashes, itching, and round patchy alopecia, with one cat showing a lump and scar on the neck. One cat has a high fever (103.7°F) and decreased appetite. Skin cytology and blood tests were performed to identify bacterial or fungal infections. Treatment includes topical antibiotics and antifungals, omega fatty acid supplementation, flea and tick control, and deworming. Owner advised to provide wet food, avoid sudden diet changes, and keep cats indoors during treatment. Follow-up is planned after diagnostic results to guide further management.

customer_instructions: Administer medications as prescribed, preferably mixing tablets with food or using syrup forms; apply topical ointments and sprays as directed; separate cats for 30 minutes after topical application to prevent licking; provide wet food and gradually transition diets by mixing old and new food; avoid harsh chemicals in areas where cats rest; complete full antibiotic course if started; monitor temperature, appetite, and behavior; keep cats indoors during treatment; report any worsening or new symptoms promptly.
